findings.title: Use a valid installer URL
findings.whyItBreaks: The URL currently returns HTTP 404 with an HTML body. Because curl lacks --fail, it pipes that body into sh, which exits with a syntax error and prevents the image from building.

findings.title: Fail the build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: If curl fails before returning a body, the pipeline reports sh's exit status. sh exits successfully on empty input, so the Docker RUN can succeed without running the installer.

findings.title: Replace the placeholder installer URL
findings.whyItBreaks: The URL currently returns HTTP 404 with an HTML page. Because curl is not given --fail, it pipes that page to sh; sh fails to parse it and the Docker build stops at this RUN.

findings.title: Propagate download failures before running the installer
findings.whyItBreaks: If curl encounters a transport failure before producing output, sh receives empty input and exits successfully. The pipeline reports sh's status, so Docker can accept an image build where the installer never ran.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Each image build executes the current response from a remote URL with the Docker build user's privileges, which are root by default. The script version and contents are not pinned or verified, so a changed or compromised source can run arbitrary commands during the build and alter the image.

findings.title: Propagate installer download failures to the image build
findings.whyItBreaks: If curl fails to transfer the script, it exits nonzero but sh receives empty input and exits successfully. The pipeline reports sh's status, so Docker can accept the layer and continue without running the installer.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error in the public helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing when the key is absent, but this helper discards that error and returns "". A caller therefore receives the same result for a missing key and a key explicitly mapped to an empty string.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key signal in the public wrapper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key at line 10, but this exported wrapper discards that error and returns an empty string. Callers cannot distinguish an absent key from a present key whose value is empty.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each job now sends from a goroutine, but Run does not wait for those goroutines. A caller that closes results after Run returns can race with a pending send and panic; callers can also observe Run complete before all results are delivered. The previous loop returned only after each send completed.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Run now launches one sender per job and returns without waiting. A caller that closes results after Run returns can race with a pending send and panic; callers can also observe incomplete output after the call.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Run now starts one goroutine per job and returns without waiting for any send. A caller that closes results or stops receiving after Run returns can cause a send-on-closed-channel panic or leave goroutines blocked; previously Run returned only after all sends completed.

findings.title: Require both admin status and a tenant match
findings.whyItBreaks: The `||` grants permission to any same-tenant user and to an admin targeting a different tenant. Either case bypasses the prior requirement that the user be an admin in the record's tenant.

findings.title: Require both admin status and matching tenant for deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: The new OR grants deletion to a non-admin in the record's tenant and to an admin from another tenant. Both cases were denied by the previous AND check, so this weakens the deletion authorization boundary and can permit unauthorized or cross-tenant data deletion.

findings.title: Require admin status and a matching tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: When a non-admin has the record's tenant, this returns true; an admin from another tenant also gets true. Callers using this exported predicate to authorize deletion can therefore permit unauthorized same-tenant and cross-tenant deletes.

The report is internally inconsistent; the base implementation fetched artifacts at the reported commit.

findings.title: Set the header count from the filtered rows

findings.title: Count only live rows in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, the returned manifest omits its row but still reports entries.length at src/manifest.ts:22. For example, one stale entry produces entry-count: 1 with zero data rows, so the header does not describe the manifest contents.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The snapshot reports the requested channel's commit at line 16 but loads files from the stable branch. When those branches point to different commits, the snapshot's files do not match its commit.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the returned base revision

findings.title: Return gateway submission failures from Charge
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge logs it and then returns nil. Callers cannot distinguish a failed charge from a successful one. Charge is exported, so this breaks its error-reporting contract even though this repository has no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Keep settings cache entries tenant-scoped
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A fetches a setting, it is cached under `settings:<name>`. A request for the same name by tenant B hits that entry and returns tenant A’s value without calling B’s store, leaking tenant-specific data or applying the wrong configuration.

findings.title: Keep tenant identity in the cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level cache is shared across tenants. After tenant A fetches a setting, the key `settings:<name>` makes `cache.get(key) !== undefined` pass for tenant B too, so B receives A’s value without calling `store.fetch` for B. This can expose tenant-scoped settings and apply the wrong configuration.

findings.title: Include tenantId in the settings cache key

After settingsFor fetches a value for tenant A, a call for tenant B with the same name returns A’s cached value without calling store.fetch for B. The SettingsStore contract accepts tenantId, so tenant-specific values can cross tenant boundaries.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 ms, but retry still multiplies it by 1,000 before sleeping at src/jobs/retry.ts:12. The first retry waits 1,000,000 ms (16m40s), and the capped delay becomes 30,000,000 ms (8h20m), instead of 1–30 seconds.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds after changing backoff units
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry passes backoff(a) * 1000 to a sleep function that already accepts milliseconds. Its first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (16 minutes 40 seconds) instead of 1,000 ms; the capped delay becomes 30,000,000 ms (8 hours 20 minutes) instead of 30 seconds.

findings.title: Propagate file close errors from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: After a successful flush, the deferred Close error is discarded and Save returns only the flush result. If the filesystem reports a write failure on Close, callers receive nil and may treat an unsuccessful save as successful. Before this change, the successful path returned f.Close(). Save is exported, so this error-conflating behavior affects its public contract even though the repository has no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Return close errors from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred Close error is discarded. If Flush succeeds but Close reports a delayed write or commit failure, Save returns nil and callers cannot tell that saving failed.

findings.title: Return file close errors from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: After Flush succeeds, the deferred Close error is discarded and Save returns nil. Close can report a delayed write or storage error; before this change, Save returned that error, allowing callers to distinguish failed persistence from success.

findings.title: Include the page’s final row
findings.whyItBreaks: range excludes its upper bound, and the code sets that bound to end - 1. For rows ['a', 'b', 'c'] with page_size=3, it returns only ['a', 'b']; every nonempty page loses its last row. render_page and summarize therefore omit rows too.

findings.title: Preserve the existing keyword parameter names
findings.whyItBreaks: The public functions rename parameters that existing callers can pass by keyword: for example, clamp(n=2, lo=1, hi=3) now raises TypeError. The same break affects page_count(total=..., size=...), page_window(rows=..., page=..., size=...), render_page(rows=..., page=..., size=...), and summarize(rows=..., size=...). The repository has no in-repo keyword callers, but these module-level functions are public.

findings.title: Include the final row in every page window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) range, but range(start, end - 1) stops before the last row. For example, a two-row page returns only its first row; render_page and summarize therefore omit rows from their output.

findings.title: Include the final row in each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: The half-open bounds end at `end`, but `range(start, end - 1)` excludes the page’s last row. A page size of 1 returns no rows, and render_page and summarize consequently omit data.

findings.title: Preserve existing public keyword parameter names
findings.whyItBreaks: Callers using the previously accepted `page_count(total=..., size=...)` keywords now get a TypeError because the public function accepts `total_rows` and `page_size`. The same parameter renaming also breaks prior keyword calls to clamp, page_window, render_page, and summarize.

findings.title: Return cache entries only while they are fresh
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition returns the value only when its age is greater than ttlMs. A fresh entry is deleted and reported missing; an expired entry is returned and left cached.

findings.title: Remove every completed job
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing while forEach advances indices skips shifted elements. For [doneA, doneB], removing index 0 shifts doneB to index 0, then iteration advances to index 1 and leaves doneB in the returned array.

findings.title: Return cached values only before expiry
findings.whyItBreaks: For an entry younger than ttlMs, the condition is false and get deletes it as a miss. Once the entry is older than ttlMs, the condition is true and get returns the expired value.

findings.title: Remove adjacent completed jobs during pruning
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing the array during forEach shifts the next item into the current index while iteration advances. For example, two adjacent completed jobs leave one completed job in the returned array.

findings.title: Return fresh cache entries and discard expired ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The comparison is reversed. With ttlMs=1000, a value read shortly after set has elapsed < 1000, so this branch is skipped and the entry is deleted; after it expires, the branch returns the stale value.

findings.title: Prune adjacent completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: When two completed jobs are adjacent, splicing the first shifts the second into its index, then forEach advances past it. For example, [done A, done B] leaves done B in the returned array.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input result for averageAmount
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, reduce returns 0 and this divides 0 by 0, producing NaN instead of the previous result, 0. Callers receive a non-finite amount that propagates through further calculations.

findings.title: Sort a copy when selecting the busiest row
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates rows in place. Previously the function sorted a copy, so callers that reuse the input now observe it reordered by amount.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average result
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, reduce returns 0 and this divides by 0, so averageAmount([]) now returns NaN instead of the previous 0. Callers receive a different, unusable numeric result for this input.

findings.title: Keep busiest from reordering the caller’s array
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates rows in place. Calling busiest now changes the caller’s array order; the previous implementation sorted a copy, so callers could rely on their input order remaining intact.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input result for averageAmount
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, the total is 0 and the length is 0, so this returns NaN. The previous implementation returned 0, and callers of this exported function now receive a different, unusable numeric result for empty input.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's row order in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates its receiver. This now reorders the caller's rows while finding the busiest row; the previous implementation sorted a copy, so callers retaining the input array observe a new side effect.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before selecting top players
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator sorts numbers by their string forms. For input scores [2, 10], sorting and reversing produces [2, 10], so with n=1 the cutoff is 2 and topPlayers can return the score-2 player instead of the score-10 player.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before selecting the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() compares numbers as strings by default. For input scores [9, 10], sorting and reversing produces [9, 10]; with n=1, the cutoff becomes 9, so topPlayers can return the score-9 player instead of the score-10 player. formatBoard then presents that player as rank 1.

findings.title: Keep score sorting numeric
findings.whyItBreaks: Without a comparator, sort orders numbers by their string forms. For scores 9 and 80, the reversed result is [9, 80]; with n=1 the cutoff is 9, so topPlayers can return the 9-point player instead of the 80-point player. formatBoard displays that incorrect selection.

findings.title: Restore constant-time webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Python string equality can stop at the first differing character, exposing signature-prefix timing information to repeated callers. The handle path returns 401 for a failed comparison and invokes the processor when it succeeds, so a caller able to measure responses may use the timing leak to help forge a valid webhook signature.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: The ordinary string comparison can stop at the first mismatching character. Repeated checks with caller-controlled signatures can reveal the matching prefix and recover the HMAC for a payload; handle then passes that payload to the processor.

findings.title: Use constant-time comparison for webhook signatures
findings.whyItBreaks: String equality can take longer when an attacker-supplied signature shares a longer prefix with the expected HMAC. An attacker who can submit signatures and observe response timing may use that difference to infer the signature. The previous hmac.compare_digest call avoided content-dependent comparison timing.

findings.title: Keep both balance updates inside the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction now ends after the ledger insert, before either balance update. If a balance update fails, the ledger insert is already committed; if the credit update fails after the debit succeeds, the debit can also remain committed. The previous code kept all three writes in the same transaction.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits after inserting the ledger row at line 23. If either balance update then fails, the ledger entry is already committed while balances are stale or partially updated.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits after recording the ledger entry, then the balance updates run outside it. If either update fails, the transfer raises after the ledger entry has committed; the ledger and account balances can disagree.

findings.title: Keep billing-day bucketing independent of host timezone
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation used UTC getters; this uses local getters, so the same instant can map to different billing dates on hosts with different timezones. For example, in a UTC−08 timezone, 2025-01-01T00:30:00Z maps to 2024-12-31. sameBillingDay can consequently return false for two instants on the same UTC day when they fall on opposite sides of local midnight.

findings.title: Preserve UTC billing-day boundaries
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation used UTC getters; this uses local getters. On a host in America/Los_Angeles, 2026-09-23T00:30:00Z now produces 2026-09-22 instead of 2026-09-23. Billing-day keys and sameBillingDay results can therefore vary with the server timezone.

findings.title: Preserve UTC billing-day extraction
findings.whyItBreaks: These local-time getters replace UTC getters, so the same Date can produce different billing-day strings on hosts with different timezones. For example, in America/Los_Angeles, 2024-01-01T07:30:00Z and 2024-01-01T08:30:00Z both previously mapped to 2024-01-01; they now map to 2023-12-31 and 2024-01-01. sameBillingDay then returns false for two instants on the same UTC billing day.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The memo is shared across calls. After readProfile("tenant-a", "alice", ...) caches a profile, readProfile("tenant-b", "alice", ...) hits the same key and returns tenant A’s profile without calling the second fetcher. This can expose the wrong tenant’s profile and display name.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After caching a profile for one tenant, a call for the same account in another tenant hits the same key and returns the first tenant's profile without calling that tenant's fetcher.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level cache is now keyed only by account. After caching a profile for one tenant, a read for the same account in another tenant hits that entry and returns the first tenant’s profile at line 16 without fetching the requested profile.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from `load`
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `missing: <key>`. The catch now returns `""`, which is indistinguishable from a legitimate stored empty string. `loadAll` therefore returns an empty entry instead of propagating the missing-key error.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing-key error and any error from store.get previously propagated. The catch now converts them to "". Since an empty string can also be a valid stored value, callers cannot distinguish missing data from success; loadAll returns an array containing "" instead of propagating the error.

findings.title: Preserve errors from missing keys
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts a missing-key error or a `store.get` exception to `""`. `loadAll` then returns that value as if loading succeeded, and callers cannot distinguish it from a key that legitimately stores an empty string. Since `load` is exported, this error-swallowing behavior also affects external callers.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config fields for retry callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported and used by the exported retry function. Existing TypeScript callers supplying { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer satisfy the interface, which now requires retries and timeout. Existing JavaScript callers pass undefined as config.timeout; adding it to Date.now() produces NaN, so the deadline check never returns and the timeout is ignored.

findings.title: Propagate exhausted callback failures from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: When every callback invocation throws, this catch discards each exception and the function returns void after the loop. Callers cannot distinguish total failure from a successful callback, so they may proceed as if the operation succeeded.

findings.title: Preserve the existing retry config shape
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported. Existing TypeScript callers passing { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer satisfy it because retries and timeout are required. JavaScript callers using that shape get undefined for config.timeout; Date.now() + undefined produces NaN, so the deadline check at line 10 never expires and retries can exceed the configured timeout.

findings.title: Propagate the final background retry error
findings.whyItBreaks: When fn throws, this catch discards the error. If attempts run out, or the deadline prevents another attempt, retryBackground returns normally with void. Callers cannot distinguish exhausted failure from success.

findings.title: Run the initial call before counting retries
findings.whyItBreaks: The public `retries` setting counts total calls, not retries after the initial call. With `retries: 1`, `fn` runs only once; with `retries: 0`, it never runs.

findings.title: Propagate the final background retry failure
findings.whyItBreaks: When `fn` throws on every attempt, each exception is discarded and the function returns normally after exhaustion or when the deadline check exits. Callers cannot distinguish failure from success.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config fields for retry callers
findings.whyItBreaks: `Config` is exported and previously accepted `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }`. Existing typed consumers now lack required `retries` and `timeout` fields. If an old-shaped config reaches `retry` at runtime, `config.timeout` is `undefined`, the deadline becomes `NaN`, and the timeout guard never rejects another attempt.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading their length
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed prop type accepts numbers, but numbers have no `length` property. Passing a valid numeric value produces `len=undefined`; TypeScript also rejects accessing `length` on the `string | number` union.

findings.title: Convert numeric values before reading their length
findings.whyItBreaks: The updated public prop type accepts numbers, but numbers have no `length` property. Passing a number therefore renders the input default value as `len=undefined`.

findings.title: Normalize numeric values before reading their length
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported prop type now accepts numbers, but numbers have no `.length`. For `value={42}`, this computes `len=undefined`; TypeScript also rejects `.length` on the `string | number` union.

findings.title: Stop printing the deployment token
findings.whyItBreaks: This writes TOKEN to the workflow log. GitHub usually redacts registered secrets, but its documentation says redaction is not guaranteed; an unredacted value would be visible to people with access to the run log.

findings.title: Do not print the deployment token
findings.whyItBreaks: The shell expands TOKEN into workflow output. GitHub redacts secrets, but that protection is not guaranteed for structured or multiline values; if redaction misses, people with access to the run logs can read the credential and use its granted access.

findings.title: Restore the larger buffer for git output
findings.whyItBreaks: The git helper now uses spawnSync’s 1 MiB default maxBuffer. A PR whose diff exceeds that size causes the diff call at line 140 to fail before review starts; the previous 64 MiB limit handled such diffs.

findings.title: Preserve the 64 MiB limit for Git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. When the git diff output exceeds that limit, spawnSync reports an error and git() throws. This happens while constructing the bundle, before runGithub's review try/catch, so the review and check are not posted for large PRs.

findings.title: Preserve enough buffer for large Git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: The full PR patch is captured by git() at line 140. Without an explicit maxBuffer, spawnSync uses its 1 MiB default; a larger diff makes the command fail and git() throw before review(bundle) is called, so that PR receives no review result. The previous 64 MiB limit allowed these patches.

findings.title: Keep Codex review runs in a read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Without the explicit read-only mode, Codex can inherit `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access` from its configuration. This invocation sets `cwd` to `opts.repoPath`, so a prompt can cause Codex to modify the reviewed tree; with full access it may also write outside that directory. The previous argument prevented those writes.

findings.title: Keep PR review runs in read-only mode
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `-s read-only` override was the wrapper's guarantee that Codex could not write during a review. Without it, Codex can inherit a `workspace-write` setting from its configuration or trust state; its working directory is `opts.repoPath` at line 24, so model-generated commands can modify the repository being reviewed.

findings.title: Keep Codex executions in read-only mode
findings.whyItBreaks: Without the explicit read-only flag, Codex resolves its sandbox from configuration; its permission resolver defaults trusted projects to workspace-write, which permits edits in the working directory ([resolver](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/config/src/config_toml.rs), [workspace-write policy](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/prompts/templates/permissions/sandbox_mode/workspace_write.md)). This wrapper sets the child working directory to opts.repoPath at line 24, so a write-capable policy lets the review run modify the checkout.

findings.title: Diff against the PR head from its merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the base-branch tip and the PR branch has diverged, diffing that tip directly against HEAD includes changes made only on the base branch instead of limiting the review to changes since the merge base. Also, when PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checked-out HEAD, the patch and changed-file set describe HEAD while the bundle and GitHub review/check target PR_HEAD_SHA. The prior code diffed the merge base against headSha.

findings.title: Diff against the merge base and PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current base-branch commit and the PR head does not contain later base commits, diffing that base tree directly against local HEAD includes those base-only changes in the review patch and changed-file set. The result is passed to review() and then posted against headSha, which may be PR_HEAD_SHA, so unrelated changes can produce findings or mislocated inline comments.

findings.title: Build the reviewed patch from the PR head's merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA names a target branch commit advanced beyond the PR's fork point, diffing from it includes base-only changes in the patch and changed-file set. When PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checkout's HEAD, the patch describes the checkout instead of the PR head, while the review and check are posted against headSha at line 178. The previous code computed the merge base and diffed against headSha.

findings.title: Keep prompt substitutions literal
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets tokens such as $& in its replacement string. If bundle.patch contains code like .replace("x", "$&"), this line inserts {{PATCH}} in place of that token in the critic prompt, so the critic reviews corrupted diff content. The direct replacements on lines 25 and 32 have the same issue for bundle and findings content.

findings.title: Preserve patch text literally in the critic prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: Passing bundle.patch as a replacement string makes String.replace interpret sequences such as $&, $' and $$ instead of preserving them. For example, a patch containing $& inserts the {{PATCH}} marker in place of that text, so runCodex at line 34 receives corrupted or missing patch content. The replacements at lines 25 and 32 have the same issue for bundle and findings text.

findings.title: Preserve literal replacement tokens in patch text
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets tokens in its replacement string. If bundle.patch contains `$&`, the inserted patch loses those characters and gets `{{PATCH}}` instead; `$'` and $` can also insert prompt text. The corrupted critic prompt is then sent to runCodex at line 34, so the reviewer may miss defects in the actual diff. The same change also affects the bundle and findings replacements at lines 25 and 32.

findings.title: Pin fallback reviews to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: If the JSON request fails and the PR head advances before the fallback succeeds, this request omits commit_id. GitHub defaults an omitted commit_id to the latest PR commit, so a stale REQUEST_CHANGES result can be applied to code the review did not analyze. [GitHub's create-review API docs](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/pulls/reviews) confirm this default.

findings.title: Preserve the reviewed SHA in the fallback review
findings.whyItBreaks: postReview receives the SHA used for the review at line 183, but this fallback no longer sends it. If the first request fails and the PR advances before the fallback, GitHub defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit. The review can then be attributed to a commit that was not reviewed.

findings.title: Keep fallback reviews pinned to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: `runGithub` builds the review for `headSha` and passes that SHA to `postReview` (lines 141, 170–183). If the JSON request fails after the PR advances, this fallback omits `commit_id`, so GitHub attaches the review to the PR’s most recent commit, which may not be the commit reviewed. This can apply a `REQUEST_CHANGES` review to an unanalyzed commit. GitHub documents that an omitted `commit_id` defaults to the most recent PR commit: [Create a review for a pull request](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/pulls/reviews#create-a-review-for-a-pull-request).

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of emitting fallback records
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid severity or category, missing required text, and non-positive line numbers used to throw. They now produce a Finding with fallback values such as P1, bug, empty strings, or line 0. normalizeReview maps each input finding through this function, so malformed records are returned as if normalization succeeded and callers cannot distinguish them from valid findings.

findings.title: Preserve the exported strict-mode parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function no longer accepts its strict boolean parameter. TypeScript consumers calling normalizeReview(review, false) will fail to compile, and JavaScript consumers lose the prior mode that filtered malformed findings instead of throwing. The repository has no in-repo callers to migrate.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of manufacturing P1 records
findings.whyItBreaks: With an invalid severity and otherwise valid fields, normalizeFinding now returns severity P1, which normalizeReview emits as an ordinary finding at line 131. Previously the invalid severity threw, so callers could distinguish malformed output from a real P1 finding. Missing required fields also become empty strings or line 0.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, invalid severity or missing required fields caused normalizeFinding to throw, and normalizeReview's default strict path propagated that error. Now normalizeFinding({}) returns a P1 finding with an empty file and line 0; normalizeReview includes it in the successful result. Callers can no longer distinguish malformed input from a real finding, and may present or act on fabricated data.

findings.title: Keep the repository explicit before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so these commands run before the checkout step. With REPO removed and no -R option, gh pr view must infer the repository from the workspace or GH_REPO. A clean runner workspace has neither, so ref resolution fails and the manual review never starts.

findings.title: Keep the repository explicit when resolving dispatched PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so these commands run before any checkout and without a local Git remote or GH_REPO. gh pr view cannot infer the repository and returns an error; command substitution hides its nonzero status, and echo writes empty head/base outputs. Checkout then receives an empty ref and the review step receives empty PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA, so the workflow may review the dispatch ref instead of the requested PR.

findings.title: Keep the repository explicit when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, and this step runs before the PR checkout. In a fresh workspace, gh pr view with only a PR number has no current repository context: GH_TOKEN authenticates the request, while GH_REPO or -R selects the repository ([gh CLI environment docs](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_help_environment), [gh pr view docs](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_pr_view)). The failed command substitution is wrapped by echo, which succeeds and writes empty head/base outputs; the later checkout and reviewer receive no resolved PR SHAs.

findings.title: Reject malformed review payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, invalid input or missing required fields threw a malformed-review error. Now this exported function returns a RawReview with empty defaults, so callers cannot distinguish malformed output from a valid review with no findings or checks.

findings.title: Reject malformed review output instead of fabricating an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: For example, normalizeReview({}) now returns a RawReview with an empty summary and empty findings, checked, and residual risks instead of throwing. Callers of this exported function can no longer distinguish malformed analyzer output from a legitimate empty review.

findings.title: Reject malformed reviews instead of returning empty results
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs that previously threw for a non-object or missing required fields now return a RawReview with empty defaults. Callers cannot distinguish malformed review output from a legitimate empty review and may treat the failed review as having no findings.

findings.title: Check out the requested PR on manual runs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, the pull_request context is absent, so this expression selects github.ref: the branch chosen for the workflow run. The workflow then invokes the reviewer with the separately supplied PR number at line 47, while the file comment says self-review uses the checked-out PR's own source. If that PR head differs from the dispatch branch, the review runs with the wrong reviewer code.

findings.title: Resolve the selected PR before checking out
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, pull_request.head.sha is absent, so checkout uses github.ref, the branch selected for the workflow run. The later command still targets the input PR number, but runs src/cli.ts from that dispatch branch. This breaks the file's stated self-review behavior when the selected PR head differs from the dispatch branch.

findings.title: Check out the PR selected by manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request.head.sha is absent, so this falls back to github.ref, which is the ref selected for the workflow run—not the head of the PR supplied as pr_number. The CLI then runs src/cli.ts from that checkout (line 47). The previous workflow resolved the input PR's head SHA before checkout.

findings.title: Preserve the larger buffer for Git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Node’s spawnSync default maxBuffer is 1 MiB. runLocal captures the full `git diff` output at line 100; when that patch exceeds the limit, the child is terminated and its output truncated. The status check at line 12 then throws, preventing review of a valid large change. The previous 64 MiB limit allowed such diffs.

findings.title: Preserve capacity for large git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit maxBuffer, spawnSync uses Node’s 1 MiB default. When the diff output exceeds that limit, git() sees a nonzero or null status and throws; runLocal then aborts while capturing the patch at line 100, before review() is called. The previous 64 MiB limit allowed these reviews.

findings.title: Restore the 64 MiB limit for git output
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer restores spawnSync’s 1 MiB default. runLocal uses this helper to capture `git diff` at line 100; when a patch exceeds the limit, the subprocess fails and runLocal throws before review receives the patch. The previous 64 MiB limit allowed such patches.

findings.title: Keep review failures blocking required checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review throws, this posts the named Needlefish Check Run as neutral. GitHub treats neutral as a successful required status check, so a branch protection rule requiring Needlefish can allow a PR to merge despite the summary saying it did not pass. The workflow's nonzero exit does not change this separate Check Run's conclusion. [GitHub status check documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/reference/status-checks)

findings.title: Pin all review inputs to one PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: `headSha` comes from one PR API request, `gh pr diff` independently reads the moving PR, and the bundle's repository path and changed-file set still come from the local checkout. If the PR advances between those reads, Needlefish can review one revision's patch using another revision's source and post the result to the SHA from the first request.

findings.title: Keep review failures as failing check runs
findings.whyItBreaks: When review throws, the published check now concludes `neutral`. If Needlefish is a required status check, GitHub accepts `neutral` as a successful required status, so the PR may merge despite the review error; the remaining process exit code does not make this check fail. [GitHub documents neutral as a successful required status](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/troubleshooting-required-status-checks).

findings.title: Keep review errors as a failing check
findings.whyItBreaks: A branch protection rule requiring the API-created Needlefish check can treat a neutral conclusion as non-failing, so a review error may satisfy the required check and allow a merge. The summary says the review did not pass, but the gate reads the conclusion. The nonzero process exit at line 196 only preserves failure for callers that also require the enclosing job.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow checks out the PR head, then invokes its src/cli.ts with GH_TOKEN. A PR can change that source to suppress or forge its review and use the token, which has pull-requests:write and checks:write permissions. This also executes PR-controlled code on the self-hosted runner.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Run installation from a checkout containing the tool
findings.whyItBreaks: This step now runs at the PR checkout root. The head tree contains only `.github/workflows/review.yml` and `.needlefish/answers.json`; it has no `package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, or `src/cli.ts`. `pnpm install` therefore fails, and the CLI path on line 59 is absent, so reviews cannot run.

findings.title: Do not execute PR-controlled reviewer code with write credentials
findings.whyItBreaks: Same-repository PRs pass the job condition, and this command executes the checked-out PR head on a self-hosted runner. The step also exposes `GITHUB_TOKEN` as `GH_TOKEN`; the workflow grants it `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write`. A PR can change `src/cli.ts` to exfiltrate that token or run arbitrary commands on the runner before merge.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Keep PR-controlled code out of the privileged reviewer job
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow checks out the PR head and executes its src/cli.ts with GH_TOKEN in the environment; that token has pull-requests:write and checks:write permissions. A malicious PR can use it to alter PRs or checks, and the job runs on a self-hosted runner. The workflow_dispatch branch of the job condition also allows reviewing an arbitrary PR number, including a fork PR.

findings.title: Run the CLI from a checkout that contains its source
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head commit contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no src/cli.ts, package.json, or pnpm-lock.yaml. This command therefore cannot resolve the CLI or its installed tsx binary, so the review job fails.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Preserve normalization of noncanonical severity strings
findings.whyItBreaks: A raw severity such as "p0" or " P1 " was previously normalized to P0 or P1. The exact-match check now rejects it and returns P3. normalizeReview passes raw findings through this function at line 132, so a high-priority finding becomes indistinguishable from a genuine P3 finding.

findings.title: Preserve case and whitespace normalization for severities
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview passes each raw finding to normalizeFinding at src/shared/schema.ts:132. A raw severity such as " p1 " now fails the exact includes check and becomes P3; before this change, trimming and uppercasing returned P1. This misclassifies a high-priority finding as the lowest priority.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex child process
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the filtered env and omitting spawnSync's env option makes the child inherit process.env, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. Codex can read those credentials while processing a prompt or repository content, exposing them through its output or tools.

findings.title: Strip GitHub credentials before spawning Codex
findings.whyItBreaks: With env omitted, spawnSync inherits process.env, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. Codex can read those credentials through shell commands, so prompt-controlled review content can expose or use them; the base version explicitly removed all three.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: With the explicit environment filtering removed, spawnSync inherits process.env. The Codex process and its child commands can read GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN; an adversarial prompt can ask the child to return those values, and runCodex returns its output.

findings.title: Restore the fork PR guard before using the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the same-repository condition allows fork PRs to start this job on a self-hosted runner. The job checks out the PR author's head at line 23, installs its dependencies at line 28, and runs its src/cli.ts at line 34. A fork author can therefore execute untrusted code on the trusted runner and potentially access its credentials or environment.

findings.title: Keep fork PR code off the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the same-repository condition lets pull_request events from forks reach this job. It checks out the PR head, installs its dependencies, and runs its src/cli.ts. A contributor can therefore execute arbitrary code on the self-hosted runner and access resources available to that host.

findings.title: Keep fork PR code off the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork pull requests trigger this job, which checks out the PR head, installs its dependencies, and runs its CLI. That gives untrusted PR code execution on the self-hosted runner, where it can access the runner's environment and files.

findings.title: Preserve zero-delay runner shutdown settings
findings.whyItBreaks: When either shutdown environment variable is set to "0", this condition rejects it and substitutes the positive fallback: 5000 ms for the SIGTERM grace period or 2000 ms after SIGKILL. The timers then wait that fallback at lines 123–124, so an explicit zero-delay setting no longer takes effect; the base implementation accepted zero.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner cleanup delays
findings.whyItBreaks: When NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0, this change substitutes the 5000 ms fallback, so a timed-out process that ignores SIGTERM can run for five more seconds before SIGKILL at line 124. When NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0, it substitutes 2000 ms, delaying completion at line 123. Both timer calls accept zero as an immediate delay, and the previous parser preserved it.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner kill delays
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous parser accepted 0, so setting NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 scheduled SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM, and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 stopped waiting immediately after SIGKILL. This change maps both values to their defaults (5 seconds and 2 seconds), so explicitly configured zero delays can leave a timed-out runner or an escaped descendant holding pipes open longer than configured.

findings.title: Keep uncovered changed files in the deep-review pass
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the six selected hotspots are reviewed by the loop. If a changed file is absent from those hotspots, it receives no deep review and no residual risk is recorded. The base version appended every uncovered changed file as a tail hotspot.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks reported by deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass can report residual risks, including blocking review gaps, but the merged candidate now always gives the critic an empty list. The critic therefore cannot distinguish those reported gaps from a clean deep pass, and the returned result contains only risks the critic independently recreates.

findings.title: Keep distinct findings with different failure explanations
findings.whyItBreaks: Findings with the same file, start line, category, and normalized title now share a key even when their whyItBreaks text describes different defects. The map retains only one of them, dropping a distinct finding; the previous key included a normalized whyItBreaks prefix.

findings.title: Retain the uncovered-file deep-review fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the six highest-risk hotspots are reviewed. Without the removed fallback, changed files outside those hotspots never reach the deep pass and are not reported as unreviewed, so defects in those files can be missed silently.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual risks to the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep pass can return a blocking residual risk, but candidateMerged now always supplies an empty list to the critic. The critic receives no record of that uncertainty and can produce a result that omits the blocker.

findings.title: Keep distinct reasons in the deduplication key
findings.whyItBreaks: Findings with the same file, line, category, and first 60 normalized title characters now collide even when their whyItBreaks text describes different defects. The Map retains only one, so the critic never receives the other finding.

findings.title: Preserve deep review coverage for every changed file
findings.whyItBreaks: The six-hotspot cap remains, but the uncovered-file fallback was deleted. Any changed file omitted by the mapper or outside the selected hotspots never enters a deep-review prompt, so its defects can be absent from the generated review.

findings.title: Forward residual risks from each deep pass
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass can return residual risks, but the merged critic input now always sets them to an empty array. The critic therefore cannot account for those unresolved or blocking risks, and the final result may omit them.

findings.title: Keep distinct findings with different causes
findings.whyItBreaks: Findings at the same file, line, and category now collide when their normalized titles share the first 60 characters, even if their whyItBreaks describe distinct failure modes. The map retains only one, dropping the other before the critic sees it.

findings.title: Preserve the requested focus in large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: When a patch exceeds 30,000 characters or changes more than 10 files, review() uses reviewLarge. That path no longer substitutes bundle.focus into each deep prompt, so a non-null requested focus is lost and the review can miss findings in the requested area.

findings.title: Preserve focus instructions in large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review path no longer substitutes bundle.focus into the deep prompt, so a caller-supplied focus is omitted and those reviews run without the requested direction. The small-review path still serializes the full bundle, so this regression is limited to large reviews.

findings.title: Preserve focus in large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: For bundles over 30,000 patch characters or 10 changed files, reviewLarge handles the review. Removing the FOCUS substitution means a supplied bundle.focus no longer reaches each deep review; the map bundle also no longer includes it. Large reviews therefore ignore the caller's requested focus, while reviewSmall still sends the full bundle.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the minute count
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119900 ms, the new code computes 1 minute and 60 seconds, displaying `1m 60s`; for 59900 ms it displays `60s`. The previous implementation normalized rounded seconds into the minute count.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the minute count
findings.whyItBreaks: Rounding the remainder can produce 60 seconds without increasing minutes. For 119500 ms, this renders as "1m 60s"; the previous calculation rendered "2m 0s". The same issue renders 59500 ms as "60s" instead of "1m 0s". Both per-call and total durations use this formatter.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: At 59,500 ms, minutes is 0 and seconds rounds to 60, so the output is "60s". At 119,500 ms, it produces "1m 60s". Both per-call and total durations use this formatter, so review output can show an invalid minute/second split.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported parsePositiveInteger function now allows 0 through the guard and returns it, although its name and error message promise a positive integer. Callers can receive a value that violates the parser's contract.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported parser now returns 0 for input "0", although its name and error text promise a positive integer. Callers can therefore receive a value that should fail validation.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported parsePositiveInteger function promises a positive integer, but the changed guard accepts 0 (and -0) and returns it. Callers can receive a value that violates the public parser contract.
